stories.title: Nvidia-backed Firmus said to close books as mega IPO struggles
stories.summary: Nvidia-backed Firmus reportedly closed its IPO order books after its blockbuster listing failed to attract sufficient demand. The bookbuilding process, once expected to anchor one of Australia's largest floats, struggled to gain traction with institutional investors.
stories.why_it_matters: Even marquee backing from Nvidia could not rescue the deal, underscoring that strategic endorsements no longer guarantee IPO success for AI infrastructure names. Underwriters and sponsors across APAC will likely recalibrate valuations, and cornerstone investor expectations for similar listings.

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
Reports say it has not drawn enough support for the A$11 share price marketed to potential investors

[HONG KONG] Australian data centre company Firmus Grid has closed the books on its struggling initial public offering as investors grew increasingly concerned that the deal could be pulled, according to people familiar with the information.

The bookbuilding closed as scheduled on Thursday (Oct 8) morning in Australia, without clear indication of the price or the deal structure, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deal is private.

A representative for Firmus did not immediately comment.

The Nvidia-backed firm was looking to raise US$5.5 billion, including a greenshoe option, in one of Australia’s largest-ever IPOs.

The bookbuilding process closed amid reports the company had not attracted adequate support for the A$11 share price marketed to potential investors. That pricing implied a valuation of A$43.7 billion (US$30.4 billion).

The close of the bookbuilding process was moved up to Thursday from Friday after early indications from investors well in excess of the offer size, people familiar with the matter have said.

But some potential investors turned more cautious as they worry about existing shareholders potentially flooding the market soon after the company’s debut, people familiar with the matter have said. The overhang added to concerns over what some investors see as an aggressive pricing strategy, they said.

“I’ve never seen an IPO so polarising,” Jun Bei Liu, co-founder and lead portfolio manager at Ten Cap Investment, said on Bloomberg TV. “There was a lot of international investor interest, however, when it comes to the crunch, the demand seems like it isn’t there when they were asked to put up the capital that’s required.”

In a sign of the mounting concern, shares of Firmus backer Maas Group Holdings fell as much of 30 per cent in Sydney, the most on record.

Firmus began as a Bitcoin mining operation in Australia in 2019 and has benefited from surging demand for AI infrastructure across Asia, with a pipeline of data centre projects in Australia and Singapore.

Proceeds from the listing would fund purchases of graphics processing units for its first data centre project in Batam, Indonesia, being developed with DayOne Data Centers, as part of an eight-year partnership with Nvidia.

Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase, Morgan Stanley and Morgans Financial are acting as joint lead managers on the listing. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: South Korea's once-hot AI stocks struggle for buyers as doubts grow over memory-chip boom
stories.summary: Semiconductor hub of Taiwan gaining favour due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain
stories.content:
Semiconductor hub of Taiwan gaining favour due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain

SOUTH Korea spent much of 2026 as a poster child of the scorching global AI trade. Now, by almost every measure, the US$4.3 trillion stock market is rapidly losing relevance with investors.

Turnover has collapsed 70 per cent from its peak in late May, foreigners are retreating at the fastest pace in Asia and local retail investors are also pulling back.

The Kospi, the world’s best-performing major equities benchmark in the first half, has since lost 22 per cent to be the worst in the second half while its AI-heavy Taiwanese and US peers set new highs.

Behind the reversal is a market whose AI fortunes hinge disproportionately on Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the two memory-chip giants at the heart of the global AI supply chain.

That concentration is now a liability as investors question the durability of memory chips’ boom cycle, while the brutal leverage-driven sell-off in the summer has made some global funds hesitant to return.

“The biggest challenge I see for most investors – especially those who only recently got into Korea for the memory chip trade – is that the easy money in that theme has been made,” said Phillip Wool, head of portfolio management at Rayliant Global Advisors, adding his fund has been taking profit in South Korean AI stocks and is now underweight SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.

The two chipmakers together account for over half of Kospi’s weighting and powered its ascent earlier in 2026. Foreign funds pulled US$131 billion from South Korean stocks this year, the most among major Asian markets, according to exchange data compiled by Bloomberg.

Scepticism over memory chip demand was on full display when shares of Samsung, the world’s top producer of such semiconductors, fell on Thursday (Oct 8) despite a nearly nine-fold surge in quarterly operating profit.

South Korea is now struggling to lure buyers, a problem amplified by the nearing completion of combined 55 trillion won (US$41 billion) stock buybacks by Samsung and SK Hynix.

Repurchases by the two chipmakers accounted for the bulk of the US$23 billion worth of buy orders in the market in September, according to JPMorgan Chase.

“We have seen capital increasingly gravitate back toward US equities, contributing to ongoing foreign outflows from the Korean market,” said Richard Tang, head of research Hong Kong at Julius Baer.

Individual investors, a key force behind Kospi’s 100 per cent rally in the first half, remain elusive following the July rout.

Margin loans outstanding have hovered around 33 trillion won over the past month, after peaking at 38.6 trillion won in June, according to data from the Korea Financial Investment Association. Brokerage account balances – or investor deposits awaiting deployment – have also fallen to around 100 trillion won from a record of near 140 trillion won.

“The memory names in particular have become value names, cheap at current earnings,” said Jon Withaar, a portfolio manager at Pictet Asset Management in Singapore. “But retail and fast money hedge funds do not chase value or the concept ‘cheap’. They chase growth.”

To be sure, the declines have opened up buying opportunities for some investors who see AI spending and memory chip profitability still holding up. South Korea’s ongoing initiative to boost corporate value is also another draw. Thanks to earlier gains, Kospi is still among the best performers for 2026 overall.

Yet for those less convinced, the competing Asian semiconductor hub of Taiwan is gaining favour due to its wider and deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.

Up 70 per cent in 2026, the Taiex Index beat the Kospi by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Taiwan’s stock gains are also more broad-based, with about 10 per cent of the local gauge’s members having at least doubled in value this year. That compares to 4.7 per cent for the Kospi.

“At this point in time, we prefer to express our tactical AI exposure through Taiwan equities, which offer a more complete technology hardware ecosystem and are supported by robust spending plans from major technology companies,” said Wu Chun-Lai, head of Asia asset allocation at UBS Global Wealth Management Chief Investment Office. stories.title: Water constraints may slow Selangor data centre construction by 2027
stories.summary: BIMB Securities Research warns that new data centre investment and construction in Selangor, Malaysia, could decelerate from 2027 as water supply headroom tightens over 2027–2029. Limited water availability is expected to slow approvals for new water-intensive projects in the state.
stories.why_it_matters: Selangor has been one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing data centre hubs, so water-driven approval delays would force developers to rethink site selection, cooling designs, or shift capacity to neighbouring states. Utilities and state planners now face pressure to accelerate water infrastructure, while operators with secured supply gain a competitive edge.
stories.content:
New data centre investment and construction in Selangor, Malaysia, could slow down in 2027 due to water constraints, BIMB Securities Research said. This may lead to a temporary moderation in new data centre construction awards in 2027.Current data centre construction takes about 18-24 months for completion, the research house noted. BIMB expects new award activity to pick up again from 2028.Selangor state water utility, Air Selangor, has a planned 2,360 million litres per day (MLD) water treatment plant (WTP) pipeline. This could expand capacity by about 37 per cent through 2031.This expansion could support organic growth and projected data centre water requirements of 632 MLD. However, it will result in tight near-term supply, BIMB said.The National Water Services Commission (SPAN) stipulates a 15 per cent reserve margin for water supply in the state. The earliest completion of a WTP in the state is the Rasau WTP Stage 1 with 700 MLD capacity, expected to go onstream in 2027.BIMB noted that this new capacity will be absorbed by organic growth demand, which averages about 3 per cent per year. Despite the near-term tight headroom, the completion of Langat 2 Phase 2 (760 MLD) in 2030 and Rasau Stage 2 (700 MLD) in 2031 will lift data centre headroom to 523 MLD in 2030 and 931 MLD in 2031 respectively.In the long-term, continuing investment in WTP construction and pipeline replacements will ensure demand can be accommodated. Near-term constraints can be mitigated by lower-water cooling designs, reclaimed water supply, or a shift to other states such as Johor, BIMB said.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability
- 1 min Read

# Water constraints may slow Selangor data centre construction by 2027

New data centre investment and construction in Selangor, Malaysia, could slow down in 2027 due to water constraints, according to BIMB Securities Research. Limited water supply headroom over 2027–2029 may slow approvals for new water-intensive projects.

- Published On Oct 11, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST

## Highlights

- Selangor, Malaysia, faces potential data centre construction slowdown by 2027 due to water constraints.
- Limited water supply headroom from 2027–2029 may affect approvals for water-intensive projects.
- New construction awards expected to moderate in 2027, then pick up from 2028.
- Long-term water treatment plant projects aim to increase supply by 2030 and 2031.

stories.title: AI infrastructure growth outpaces operational staffing
stories.summary: The expansion of AI data centers is creating a gap between infrastructure deployment speed and the availability of skilled operational staff. This challenge impacts facility readiness, requiring earlier workforce planning and specialized training, according to Maksim Gavriliuk.
stories.content:
The expansion of AI data centers is creating a gap between infrastructure deployment speed and the availability of skilled operational staff. This challenge impacts facility readiness, requiring earlier workforce planning and specialized training, according to Maksim Gavriliuk.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

AI infrastructure growth is outpacing the development of experienced operational talent.

Over half of data center operators struggle to find qualified candidates, Uptime Institute reported.

New AI facilities demand specialized skills for liquid cooling and managing concentrated electrical loads.

Workforce planning must start early in data center design to address future operational needs.

The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure is outpacing the development of experienced operational talent, creating a significant challenge for data center readiness, an independent expert said.Maksim Gavriliuk, an independent digital infrastructure and data center expert, highlighted that while data centers can be designed in months and built in years, developing experienced operations engineers takes much longer. This disparity is becoming more pronounced as AI infrastructure demands grow.Uptime Institute’s 2026 Global Data Center Survey found that over half of data center owners and operators struggle to find qualified candidates for open positions. Recruitment and retention pressures are persistent, with staff turnover remaining a challenge as employees move to competing data center companies.

Skills gap in AI facilities

Technical roles, particularly in operations, mechanical, and electrical fields, are consistently difficult to fill, according to Uptime Institute’s workforce research. There is also increasing demand for controls and monitoring specialists, who are crucial for day-to-day management of dense infrastructure.Mature data center markets, including the US and Western Europe, face significant retirements among experienced technical staff. This demographic shift leads to a loss of institutional knowledge, which is difficult to replace through simple headcount additions. Uptime previously estimated global data center staffing needs would increase from two million full-time equivalents in 2019 to nearly 2.3 million by 2025, with AI further boosting demand.AI facilities introduce new operational complexities and skill requirements. Modal rack densities are rising, with many operators reporting peak racks of 30 kW or above, and AI training deployments can exceed this. Liquid cooling is becoming a core infrastructure consideration, requiring teams to manage coolant quality, leak response, and cooling distribution units.Electrical operations are also changing, with AI clusters creating concentrated loads and different operating conditions compared to traditional data halls. The distinction between IT and facilities responsibilities blurs, as cooling issues can directly impact high-value compute equipment.

Early planning and training needed

Organisations often install new technology faster than their operating models can adapt, meaning teams may lack the specific skills required for new infrastructure. Structured training and visible career paths are essential to develop existing staff and attract technicians from adjacent sectors.Operational documentation, clear procedures, and defined competencies can help transfer knowledge from experienced staff to new recruits. This is crucial in markets where data center construction has outpaced the development of local operations teams.Data center developers plan years ahead for power, land, and long-lead equipment, but staffing often enters the process too late. Workforce planning should begin at the design stage to identify required skills, recruitment sources, and training timelines. This proactive approach can mitigate the risk of operational capacity shortages once infrastructure is built.

stories.title: Agentic AI increases CPU role in enterprise infrastructure: AMD
stories.summary: Agentic AI workflows are giving central processing units (CPUs) a more meaningful role in enterprise AI infrastructure, according to AMD's Derek Dicker. This shift affects data center modernisation and rack-scale system design.
stories.content:
Agentic AI workflows are giving central processing units (CPUs) a more meaningful role in enterprise AI infrastructure, according to AMD's Derek Dicker. This shift affects data center modernisation and rack-scale system design.

Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google

Highlights

Agentic AI increases the role of CPUs in enterprise AI infrastructure, says AMD.

AMD and TCS HyperVault plan a 200 MW Helios-based AI infrastructure blueprint in India.

AMD's EPYC processors offer up to 8:1 server consolidation for data centre modernisation.

The company is developing rack-scale systems like Helios and AI deployment appliances.

Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) workflows are increasing the role of central processing units (CPUs) in enterprise AI infrastructure, according to Derek Dicker, Corporate Vice President, Enterprise Business Group at AMD.This development impacts how enterprises approach infrastructure, from consolidating older servers to designing complete systems and managing AI usage costs, Dicker told Dataquest.

AMD's AI Infrastructure Strategy

AMD's AI infrastructure strategy combines silicon design, open standards and software, and rack-scale systems. The company builds semiconductor products including CPUs, graphics processing units (GPUs), networking, and field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs).AMD also supports open standards for interoperability and open-source software, specifically the ROCm stack, across CPU and GPU segments. The company is developing rack-scale systems, with Helios being an initial example.Helios is described as a 72-GPU, highly orchestrated system with a full rack specification, designed to work with ROCm and ecosystem partners.

Server Consolidation and Inference Workloads

Enterprises often face challenges integrating AI into existing data centres that are already at capacity. AMD’s EPYC processors help address this through server consolidation.Fifth-generation EPYC products can replace up to eight older servers with a single AMD EPYC-based server. Calculations suggest a 13:1 consolidation ratio for sixth-generation products.This consolidation frees up space within existing data centre infrastructure for new AI deployments. The company also noted the growing importance of inference workloads, which are expanding dramatically and may become the dominant portion of compute utilisation.Dicker said inference will require heterogeneous computing environments, with different optimisations for client, edge, and data centre instances.

Evolving CPU Role and India Focus

The CPU's role is evolving from general compute and GPU cluster head nodes to agent orchestration. This could lead to a one-to-one CPU-to-GPU ratio for agentic AI workloads.AMD is also developing 'appliances', which are OEM or ODM systems with validated software, to help customers deploy AI infrastructure quickly. The AMD Instinct Coder is the first in a series of such appliances.In India, AMD and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), through TCS’s HyperVault subsidiary, plan to co-develop Helios-based AI infrastructure. This collaboration includes a data centre blueprint supporting up to 200 MW of capacity.AMD also has relationships with local providers for 'Make in India' OEM systems, supporting the domestic manufacturing ecosystem.The company emphasises listening to customer needs, solving pain points, and ensuring on-time product delivery as foundations for its success in enterprise computing.
